div.p: Somatic cells in mammalian semen can be a potential source of nuclei for nuclear transfer to produce cloned animals. Somatic cells recovered from avian semen could also provide a source of cells for use in chimera formation or cloning of threatened and endangered birds. This type of assisted reproductive technology is especially important when a genetically unique animal has died and the only viable genetic material available is semen cryopreserved for artificial insemination and in vitro fertilization purposes. The usefulness of somatic cells obtained from fresh and frozen mammalian semen for nuclear transfer has already been evaluated, but still remains to be accomplished for avian semen. A non-invasive, or minimally invasive, technique to conserve avian genetic diversity via somatic cell collection from fresh avian semen, to our knowledge, has not been described. The present study investigated the use of fresh semen samples from domestic chickens (Gallus domesticus) (n = 7), i.e., white leghorn (n = 4) and silkie chickens (n = 3), as a source of somatic cells, specifically fibroblast-like cells and epithelial cells, for cytological analysis and somatic cell gene banking. Ultimately, somatic cell culture was successful for two of six selected samples (33.3%), with two of four white leghorn semen samples yielding cell cultures compared to 0 of 2 silkie chicken semen samples. Further research may include applying this technique to other avian species or address the effects of cryopreservation on the viability and DNA integrity of somatic cells derived in this manner.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Somatic cells found in human semen include epithelial cells, and various major leukocyte subpopulations such as granulocytes, monocytes/macrophages, B lymphocytes, helper and suppressor/cytotoxic T lymphocytes (Phillips et al., 1978;Wolff and Anderson, 1988;Homyk et al., 1990). However, limited information is available about somatic cells in semen of livestock and companion animals. Phillips et al. (1978) reported that epithelial cultures, uncontaminated by fibroblast cells, were obtained from human semen samples. More recently, epithelial cell cultures have been obtained from eland (Nel-Themaat et al., 2007) and sheep (Liu et al., 2009) semen. However, to our knowledge the question of whether or not somatic cells can be isolated and cultured from avian semen samples has not been addressed.

Semen contains somatic cells that are a potential source of nuclei for nuclear transfer to produce genetically identical animals. For instance, some animals of high genetic value have died and the only viable genetic material available is cryopreserved semen. As has been demonstrated with bovine semen (Liu et al., 2010), growing somatic cells from fresh samples provides the knowledge to eventually be able to grow somatic cells from frozen semen. Somatic cells recovered from semen samples in this manner can be used for cytological analysis and possibly for cloning and chimera formation. If somatic cells in semen can be used successfully for somatic nuclear transfer (SCNT), then this could, in some cases, represent an extremely valuable resource for the preservation or restoration of these valuable animals. The recovery of somatic cells, specifically, epithelial cells and fibroblast-like cells (hereafter referred to as fibroblast cells), from avian semen would in effect allow for the non-invasive collection of somatic cells for cytogenetic analysis and for use in techniques such as chimera formation, iPSC creation, or cloning. The primary objective of the present investigation was to determine if a method developed for recovering mammalian somatic cells from fresh semen could be applied for isolating and propagating somatic cells from freshly collected avian semen.

div.head: Background
div.p: Non-invasive means of obtaining somatic cells are desired, both to reduce the stress and pain that may accompany invasive methods on the animals themselves and also to avoid exposure to pathogens that could jeopardize the health of an animal. With regard to birds, the scientific literature addresses the use of feathers as a non-invasive, or minimally invasive, means to conserve avian genetic diversity via somatic cell gene banking. The establishment of avian fibroblast cell lines from feather pulp has been conducted at the San Diego Zoo's Institute for Conservation Research and these cell lines were used for California condor karyotyping and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) (Romanov et al., 2009). Additionally, the use of post-hatch eggshells as a completely noninvasive means to obtain fibroblast-like cells has been reported (Kjelland and Kraemer, 2012).

The potential cryopreservation and subsequent viability of fibroblast cells is important because they are commonly a source of nuclear DNA used for SCNT in mammalian cloning, as well as chimera formation. Although cloning has not yet been performed for any avian species, there are several reports of avian chimera formation in the scientific literature, e.g., Li et al. (2002) and Song et al. (2005). In the future, the techniques investigated herein may serve as a valuable tool for the preservation of genetic material from endangered avian species.

Although still an inefficient process, nuclear transfer has been widely used to produce genetically identical animals for research and commercial purposes. The birth of Dolly in 1997 (Wilmut et al., 1997) first demonstrated that fully differentiated adult somatic cells can be reprogrammed to produce live clones. Endangered (Lanza et al., 2000;Loi et al., 2001;Li et al., 2006;Gómez and Pope, 2006;Kim et al., 2007), exotic (Williams et al., 2006), extinct (Gray and Dobson, 2009), and transgenic animals (when combined with molecular biology techniques) (Dai et al., 2002;Golding et al., 2006;Jang et al., 2006;Hao et al., 2006;Yin et al., 2008) have also been produced by nuclear transfer techniques.

Traditional cloning techniques involve visualizing chromosomes of mammalian oocytes with an inverted microscope (Yin et al., 2002), DNA staining and removal of the genetic material in preparation for nuclear transfer. Although this technique works well for the oocytes of several species, technical difficulties arise for those species whose oocytes are visually opaque. The issue of ovum opacity is especially problematic for the large and cumbersome avian ovum. The size and delicacy of the avian ovum make it somewhat difficult and awkward to manipulate while the sheer volume of the cytoplasm makes visualizing the nucleus virtually impossible (Etches, 2003). However, Sang and Sherman (2005) have already explored the possibility of enucleating avian ova and although avian cloning has not yet been achieved, some patent related information currently exists for cloning birds in the scientific literature, i.e., U.S. patent applications (Christmann, 2005;Christmann, 2006), and U.S. patent #20050015825 (Sang and Sherman, 2005). Even though the ability to clone birds has not yet been accomplished, the ability to obtain and cryopreserve somatic cells noninvasively for potential future avian cloning efforts may still be justified. Aside from the potential use of the semen isolated somatic cells in future avian cloning efforts, another possibility is using the fibroblast cells for the creation of induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs).

Induced pluripotent stem cells have been derived from endangered wildlife species with species preservation in mind (Selvaraj et al., 2011), for example, the drill (Mandrillus leucophaeus) and the nearly extinct northern white rhinoceros (Ceratotherium simum cottoni), and this may eventually facilitate reintroduction of genetic material into breeding populations (Ben-Nun et al., 2011). Recently, Lu et al. (2012) have demonstrated the generation of avian iPSCs, i.e., quail iPSCs (qiPSCs), which were clonally isolated, propagated, and were directly differentiated in culture and capable of generating live chimeric birds. Therefore, if one does not wish to use the semen for producing a hybrid, one could theoretically use the somatic cells from the semen for iPSC production and subsequent production of germline chimeric birds that could produce fertile offspring.

For rare avian species, the acquisition of fibroblastlike cells using the non-invasive techniques presented herein might be a valuable tool for both genetic analysis and conserving genetics for future assisted reproductive techniques. A scenario where this may be utilized would be a case where the bird of interest has already died, and somatic cells were never specifically collected and cryopreserved for gene banking, but cryopreserved semen samples do still exist.

div.head: Reagents
div.p: Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium/Nutrient Mixture F-12 (DMEM/F-12) was purchased from Gibco (Grand Island, NY, USA). Fetal bovine serum (FBS) was purchased from Hyclone (Logan, UT, USA). All other reagents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA) unless otherwise indicated.

div.head: Semen collection, transport, somatic cell isolation, and culture
div.p: The research herein was conducted in accordance with the Animal Care Guidelines of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Texas A&M University. Chickens were caged at a minimum density of one hen per cage, 216 inches 2 per bird, each cage having its own nipple drinker providing a readily available water supply. All feeds were manufactured at a mill located at the poultry center and formulated using current NRC (Nutritional Requirements of Chickens) guidelines. The birds were fed a standard laying mash consisting of roughly 17% protein, 3.6% calcium, and 2,866 kcal kg -1 . For internal and external parasite control, the feed contained Monensin (Coban 60, 60 active grams per ton). External parasites, such as northern fowl mites, poultry lice, and insects were controlled with a 10% permethyrin spray (Permasan). Seven ejaculates were collected from white leghorn chickens (n = 4) and silkie chickens (n = 3), at the Poultry Science Research, Teaching, and Extension Center at Texas A&M University. Two of the seven ejaculates were pooled due to small volumes, i.e., two silkie chicken semen samples, thereby producing six separate samples. All of the animals appeared to be in good health at the time of the semen collections.

Semen was expressed via manual massaging of the rooster's abdomen; similar to the method described previously in Gee et al. (2004) and Quinn and Burrows (1936). Before beginning the massage technique, feathers were trimmed away from the cloaca and the area was washed using 70% isopropyl alcohol. The semen was expelled and collected in a 10 mL glass beaker and diluted approximately 1:3 with 0.9% phosphate buffered saline (PBS) solution before transferring the sample to a 15 mL conical tube. Then, the semen sample was placed in a Styrofoam cooler with an ice pack in the bottom, and separated by a paper towel, for transport (~15 min) and subsequent preparation for processing in the laboratory.

Somatic cells were isolated and cultured as described in Liu et al. (2009) and Nel-Themaat et al. (2008a;b) with minor modifications. Briefly, each semen sample was gently layered over a 3-layer gradient column (2.5 mL each of 20%, 50%, and 90% Percoll®) in a 15 mL conical tube and centrifuged at 400g for 20 min. Cells in the 20% gradient and top half of the 50% gradient were centrifuged at least twice at 400g for 10 min. in DMEM/F12 supplemented with 100 µg mL -1 gentamicin by centrifugation. Afterwards, cell pellets were re-suspended in DMEM/F-12 supplemented with 10% FBS, 10 ng mL -1 epidermal growth factor, 30 µg mL -1 bovine pituitary extract, 5 µg mL -1 insulin, 10 ng mL -1 cholera toxin, 200 µg mL -1 gentamycin, 100 units mL -1 penicillin, 100 µg mL -1 streptomycin, and 0.25 µg mL -1 amphotericin B, and cultured in 25 cm 2 (T-25) cell culture flasks (BD Falcon, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) with vent caps (2µm pore size) at 37 ºC in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO 2 in air. Medium was changed 24 h after plating.

The cell culture flasks were checked for bacteria and/or fungi contamination daily for one week. Medium in cell culture flasks containing bacteria and/or fungi was replaced with fresh medium until contamination was eliminated. The concentration of gentamicin was decreased at each medium change from 150 µg mL -1 to 100 µg mL -1 , and finally to 50 µg mL -1 . Penicillin, streptomycin, and amphotericin B were likewise gradually excluded from the culture medium (within one to two weeks of culture). Cells were fed twice a week with fresh medium until cell culture could be verified as successful and documented using an inverted confocal microscope (Nikon Instruments Inc., Melville, NY, USA) with a fluorescence light source, 100x to 400x magnification, and NIS Elements imaging software.

div.head: RESULTS
div.p: The total number of cells obtained from each ejaculate varied, but somatic cell numbers were low and this may be due to the isolation procedure requiring further modifications in future research efforts. Basically, either no cell attachment was found (n = 3, 50%) or a few cells per ejaculate attached and started to divide (n = 3, 50%), however, one of these aforementioned cell cultures was discarded due to bacterial contamination, the silkie chicken sample. Ultimately, fibroblast cell growth was successfully obtained from two of the six samples cultured (33.3%), both from white leghorn chicken samples (Figures 1 and2). The somatic cell cultures typically initiated with bacteria and/or fungi contamination and this issue contributed to lower cell culture success.

Comparing the white leghorn chicken semen samples, only two of four provided somatic cells versus one of two for silkie chickens. In terms of somatic cell culture, two of four white leghorn chicken semen samples yielded somatic cell cultures versus zero of two silkie chicken semen samples.

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: Isolating and propagating somatic cells from frozen semen can be difficult, especially when there are a limited number of semen straws/pellets. However, perhaps nuclei of the somatic cells in frozen semen could be used for nuclear transfer even though the cell membrane and cytoplasm might be damaged as a result of the semen cryopreservation process. It is expected that the ease of obtaining somatic cells from semen samples will vary depending upon the method used for semen collection, e.g., the propensity for somatic cells to slough off into the semen during collection given the collection technique being utilized, as well as the size of the avian species being collected and the relative semen volume obtained. In the present study, small numbers of somatic cells were obtained from each ejaculate; as such, perhaps the isolation procedure may require modification in an attempt to increase the number of somatic cells isolated in future efforts. Notably, the semen sample sizes in the present study are not very large, n = 4 and n = 2 for white leghorn and silkie chickens, respectively, thereby negating the use of a statistical analysis regarding somatic cell culture success between breeds. More replicates with larger sample sizes in a future study could provide an adequate statistical power for examining the influence of breeds on the success of somatic cell isolation and cell culture.

Similar to Liu et al. (2010), although the genital area, in this case the cloaca area of the chickens, was cleaned before each semen collection; bacteria and/or fungi contamination remained a problem when growing these cells in culture. This is likely to be even more of an issue with avian semen collections due to the differences in physiology compared to animals where the semen is expressed separately from the area where the excrement also passes. We found that at 24 h post plating, a gentle washing (using culture medium) of the culture surface to which cells might have attached, helped remove bacteria and fungi; thereby decreasing the concentrations of antibiotics required in the culture medium and increasing the chances of obtaining cell growth. Perhaps more frequent medium changes during the first 24 to 72 h post plating would have helped prevent bacterial contamination as reported by Liu et al. (2010).

div.head: CONCLUSIONS
div.p: In the present study, we have demonstrated that somatic cells, specifically epithelial cells and fibroblast cells, can be isolated and cultured from fresh avian ejaculates. Some of the somatic cells cultured from avian semen ejaculates exhibited epithelial cell morphology, similar to the results found in Bos taurus (Liu et al., 2010). Unlike the case in Liu et al. (2010), where somatic cell growth was obtained from fresh bovine ejaculates with relatively high efficiency, it was not the case in the present study.

More specifically, the results demonstrate that domestic chicken semen can be a non-invasive, or minimally invasive, source of somatic cells for cell culture and as such serve for subsequent cytogenetic analysis or perhaps even for such techniques as iPSC creation. This also means that avian semen can possibly provide a source of somatic cells for chimera formation or perhaps even for future avian cloning with a special focus on critically endangered birds, e.g., Spix's macaw (Cyanopsitta spixii) or the Grenada dove (Leptotila wellsi).

Additional research on obtaining somatic cells from avian semen and refining the aforementioned cell culture technique appears warranted given the potential value of this approach for improving genetic diversity. In the future, research should be conducted on isolating somatic cells from cryopreserved avian semen of different species for assessing post-thaw cell viability and DNA integrity.
